technicalSummary:
Peltier thermal actuators and small vibration motors on the forearm, creating a “flowing” thermal illusion even though the devices stayed in fixed positions. Tested in VR scenarios.

(Original suggestion)
This study explored how to make people feel as if warmth or coldness is moving across the skin. The researchers placed Peltier thermal actuators and small vibration motors on the forearm, creating a “flowing” thermal illusion even though the devices stayed in fixed positions. They tested this in lab studies and VR scenarios, showing that moving thermal feedback could make virtual experiences feel more dynamic and immersive.

authors: Moesgen, Tim; Gowrishankar, Ramyah; Xiao, Yu

Identify experiential dimensions of heat beyond simple hot/cold descriptions

technicalSummary: This study explored how people experience intense full-body heat in a traditional Finnish sauna, rather than testing an artificial thermal device. Participants sat in an 80–90°C sauna and described their sensations through interviews, body maps, and tactile objects, focusing especially on the moment when water is poured onto hot stones. The study shows that heat experiences involve more than “hot” or “cold”, including feelings such as pressure, tingling, movement, discomfort, and body-wide distribution.

authors: Lu, Jasmine; Liu, Ziwei; Brooks, Jas; Lopes, Pedro

The stated goal of the whole system is to expand the haptic design space for interactive and VR contexts.

bodyPartsInvolved:
In the photo, it's on the face (cheeks) and forearm (ventral).
Cheeks: menthol (cooling) and capsaicin (warming) applied via a mask-style cheek patch beneath the VR headset
Forearm: all five chemicals were also tested on the forearm in Study 1 and some VR experiences in Study 2 (capsaicin warming was specifically on the cheeks in the VR walkthrough, but forearm was the primary Study 1 site)
They claim it can be worn anywhere. But it's not. You always need extra fixation to secure it. 
 
Why these parts?
The cheeks were chosen because: (1) they are a natural site for ambient facial sensations (warmth/cold) commonly associated with environmental temperature; and (2) they illustrate the system's ability to deliver chemicals to hard-to-reach locations. 
 The forearm was chosen because: (1) it is an ideal site for sensations related to arm-based UIs, which are common in VR; and (2) the sleeve form factor can be adapted to other limbs. An additional practical rationale is given: cheek skin (~38.8μm thick) absorbs chemicals faster than forearm skin (~60.9μm thick), which is relevant to the speed of thermal sensation onset.
powerEnergyConsumption: The full device consumes 0.52W at full intensity (two channels active), compared to 4–13W per small Peltier. This ~10× efficiency advantage is highlighted as a key benefit.

title: Frisson: Leveraging Metasomatic Interactions for Generating Aesthetic Chills
authors: Jain, Abhinandan; Schoeller, Felix; Zhang, Emilie; Maes, Pattie
thermalPerceptionMeasure: Questionnaire: Participants reported the perception of cold from the device on a Likert scale of 0–10 as part of the post-trial questionnaire. (number, intensity... of chills, page 153, section 4.4.4)
thermalCuePurpose:
"elicit the sensations underlying the embodied emotion of aesthetic chills"
 
 Thermal feedback is applied to simulate the somatic sensation of aesthetic chills --- the traversing cold sensation down the spine that characterises the psychogenic shiver experience. 
 
 The purpose is to trigger the emotional experience of aesthetic chills by recreating the bodily sensation that normally precedes and constitutes that emotion, grounded in the James-Lange theory of emotions and Schachter-Singer two-factor theory. 
 The thermal feedback is positioned as an "emotional prosthesis", a device that induces an embodied emotion by replicating its somatic marker. The paper specifically argues that the thermal sensation must match the individual's prior bodily experience (their "prior") in order to activate the emotional experience, and the user study tests this matching hypothesis.
mainActuatorPossibleTemperatureRange: Approximately -3°C relative to skin surface temperature
heatControlMethod: PWM control from BLE-enabled MCU; Peltiers activated in series according to spatial pattern condition
temporalParameters: Activation duration: 1s per element; total sequence duration: 3s; trigger timing: 30s into a 60s video clip
otherNote: Five Peltier elements were mounted at different spatial positions along the spine: upper left, upper centre, upper right back, middle back, and lower back. The device produced a traversing cold sensation across the back. The paper also mentions three-point and five-point device versions. Six experimental conditions were used: C1–C5 for different directional thermal patterns and C6 as no thermal feedback control. Peltiers were chosen because they can provide both heating and cooling and can be controlled individually for spatially distributed sequential stimulation.
bodyPartsInvolved:
shoulder and back: "upper left, upper center and upper right of the back, one on middle and one on the lower back". 
 
Why these locations: (Page 151)
The back/spine was chosen because aesthetic chills are physiologically localised primarily in the spinal region, with peripheral sensations in the shoulders and forearms. The authors argue this makes aesthetic chills particularly well-suited for a metasomatic device: (1) the somatic marker of aesthetic chills is spatially isolated from basic emotions (which are largely localised in the face), reducing cross-contamination with other emotional priors; (2) the spinal sensation of "chills down the spine" is the defining reported prior of the psychogenic shiver experience; and (3) the universality of this somatic marker across cultures (cited as Ref [30]) supports the choice.
